rules: Lean is the only judge. A ledger status is a claim; scripts/audit.py checks every claim against the compiled code and fails on any mismatch.
verified = the declaration builds and depends on no axiom outside propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound.
open = the declaration builds but its proof (or a proof it depends on) still uses sorry.
unformalized = there is no Lean declaration yet; the statement exists only in prose. Nothing in this state can be verified.
Adding an `axiom` to any file under Vault/ is a cheat, not a proof. The audit rejects it.
Every Lean file under Vault/ must be imported from Vault.lean or it is never built.

Every entry with `toward` carries a circularity verdict. `independent` means it is strictly weaker than the target it serves, and says why; `equivalent` means it is that target in disguise; `unassessed` means nobody has checked. Lean cannot catch a lemma that merely relocates the difficulty, so the crew runner refuses anything but `independent`.

entries.title: Infinitely many primes
entries.statement: For every natural number n there is a prime p with n <= p.
entries.notes: Canary entry. It must always audit as verified. If it does not, the door is broken.

entries.title: Sum of the first n odd numbers
entries.statement: For every natural number n, the sum over i < n of (2i + 1) equals n^2.
entries.notes: Shipped open on purpose. First job for the crew runner: provable from Mathlib by induction in a few lines. Close it with `crew/run.py practice.stage1_sum_first_odd`.

entries.title: Riemann Hypothesis
entries.statement: Every nontrivial zero of the Riemann zeta function has real part 1/2. Mathlib states this as `RiemannHypothesis`.
entries.notes: The only Millennium problem whose full statement already exists in Mathlib, which makes it the natural first formal target. Known: zeros are in the critical strip; a positive proportion lie on the line (Selberg, Levinson, Conrey); numerically verified for the first ~10^13 zeros.

entries.title: Zeta has only trivial zeros for Re s <= 0
entries.statement: If Re s <= 0 and s is not -2(n+1) for any natural n, then zeta(s) != 0.

circularity.argument: Strictly weaker than RH and provable without it. The statement constrains zeros in the half-plane re s <= 0, which RH says nothing new about: RH is a claim about the strip. The proof route in the notes uses only `riemannZeta_one_sub` and `riemannZeta_ne_zero_of_one_le_re`, both already in Mathlib and both proved without RH. A pre-RH proof exists in the literature (Titchmarsh ch. 2), so the lemma cannot encode it.

entries.notes: Classical, not in Mathlib as of v4.33.1. Sketch: apply `riemannZeta_one_sub` at 1 - s (hypotheses hold since Re(1 - s) >= 1, so 1 - s is never -n and never 1 unless s = 0, where `riemannZeta_zero` gives -1/2). Then zeta(s) = 2 (2 pi)^(-(1-s)) Gamma(1-s) cos(pi (1-s)/2) zeta(1-s). Each factor is nonzero: `riemannZeta_ne_zero_of_one_le_re` for zeta(1-s), `Complex.Gamma_ne_zero` since 1 - s is not a non-positive integer, `Complex.cos_eq_zero_iff` shows the cosine vanishes only when s is an even integer <= 0, which the hypothesis excludes (s = 0 handled separately).
references: Titchmarsh, The Theory of the Riemann Zeta-Function, ch. 2

entries.title: Nontrivial zeros lie in the open critical strip
entries.statement: If zeta(s) = 0 and s is not a trivial zero, then 0 < Re s < 1.

circularity.argument: This is the classical zero-free region, known since Hadamard and de la Vallee Poussin (1896) and used in the prime number theorem, which does not assume RH. RH is strictly stronger: this lemma delivers the open strip 0 < re s < 1, RH pins re s = 1/2 inside it. Proving the strip therefore cannot prove RH, and the converse implication is trivial.

entries.notes: Corollary: `riemannZeta_ne_zero_of_one_le_re` rules out Re s >= 1, the previous lemma rules out Re s <= 0.

entries.title: P versus NP
entries.statement: Is every decision problem whose solutions can be verified in polynomial time also solvable in polynomial time?
entries.notes: Mathlib has no complexity classes. Formalizing the statement (Turing machines or a circuit model, P, NP) is itself a lemma-sized project and must come first. Known barriers any proposal must get past: relativization (Baker-Gill-Solovay), natural proofs (Razborov-Rudich), algebrization (Aaronson-Wigderson).

entries.title: Navier-Stokes existence and smoothness
entries.statement: For smooth, finite-energy initial data in three dimensions, do the incompressible Navier-Stokes equations have a globally defined smooth solution (or a counterexample)?
entries.notes: Mathlib has Sobolev-adjacent analysis but no PDE well-posedness theory at this level. Formal statement needs function spaces and weak/strong solution definitions first.

entries.title: Yang-Mills existence and mass gap
entries.statement: Prove that quantum Yang-Mills theory on R^4 exists for any compact simple gauge group and has a mass gap Delta > 0.
entries.proposed_by: Clay official statement by Jaffe and Witten
entries.notes: The statement depends on a rigorous definition of a quantum field theory (Wightman or Osterwalder-Schrader axioms) that Mathlib does not have. Furthest from formalizable of the seven.

entries.title: Birch and Swinnerton-Dyer conjecture
entries.statement: The rank of the Mordell-Weil group of an elliptic curve over Q equals the order of vanishing of its L-function at s = 1.
entries.notes: Mathlib has elliptic curves and Mordell-Weil group structure, and general L-series machinery, but not the L-function of an elliptic curve with analytic continuation. Formalizing the statement is the first lemma.

entries.title: Hodge conjecture
entries.statement: On a projective complex manifold, every rational (p,p) cohomology class is a rational linear combination of classes of algebraic cycles.
entries.notes: Requires Hodge theory and algebraic cycles, neither of which is in Mathlib.

entries.title: Poincare conjecture (dry run)
entries.statement: Every simply connected closed 3-manifold is homeomorphic to the 3-sphere.
entries.notes: Solved by Perelman (2002-2003, prize declined 2010). Kept as a dry-run target: the answer is known, so it measures whether the pipeline can find and formalize a known proof. Mathlib has no 3-manifold theory, so the statement is unformalized.
